mod_01.text:
You receive an email saying:

"Your school account will be deleted today. Verify now."

Which detail is the strongest warning sign?
options: It creates urgency to make you act quickly
It was sent in the morning
Pretending to be trustworthy through messages to steal information or cause an unsafe action

mod_01.text:
An email says it is from your university, but the sender is:

registrar.school@gmail.com

What should concern you most?
options: It uses Gmail rather than the school's expected official domain

mod_01.text: A suspicious email asks you to log in immediately. What is safest?
options: Reply asking whether it is legitimate
Forward it to a friend first

mod_01.text:
An email shows:

Display name: University Registrar
Actual address: studentverify247@gmail.com

What should you trust when checking the sender?

You hover over "Open Student Portal" and see:

https://school-login.secure-account.xyz

What should you do?
options: Open it because HTTPS is shown
Avoid it and access the portal independently
Ask a friend to test it

mod_01.text:
An unexpected email contains:

ClassSchedule.pdf.exe

Why is this dangerous?
options: School files should always be ZIP files
.exe indicates the file can execute a program

mod_01.text: Your instructor's real name appears in an email asking you to open a project document. What would make it most suspicious?
options: The email comes from an unfamiliar domain

mod_01.text: What is the best way to verify an unexpected request from your instructor?
options: Contact the instructor using a previously known channel
Click the link to inspect it
Check whether the message uses the instructor's photo

mod_01.text:
An email claiming to be IT support asks for your password.

What should you do?
options: Send it if the address looks official
Change it and send the new password
Refuse and verify with IT independently

mod_01.text:
Consider:

https://accounts.school.edu.ph.security-check.com

Who controls the main registered domain?
You clicked a phishing link and entered your password. What should you do next?
options: Change the password using the legitimate site and report the incident
Wait to see whether anything happens

mod_01.text: Which provides the weakest evidence that an email is legitimate?
options: It uses the organization's logo and your real name
You independently confirmed the request with the sender
The domain matches the organization's official domain
The request appears inside an official account portal

mod_01.text:
An email looks legitimate but asks you to urgently download confidential documents from an unfamiliar domain.

What should determine your decision?
options: Whether the action and destination can be independently verified
Whether it contains your correct name
Social engineering using SMS or messaging apps

mod_02.text:
You receive:

"You won ₱50,000! Claim now."

You never entered a contest.

What is most likely happening?
A text asks you to send your OTP. What should you do?
options: Never provide the OTP and verify independently
Ask why they need it first

mod_02.text: A delivery message includes an unexpected link. Safest response?
options: Use the courier's official site/app independently
Ask someone else to open it

mod_02.text: Why can shortened URLs be risky?

A bank SMS appears in the same conversation thread as legitimate bank notifications.

Does that guarantee authenticity?
options: No, sender information may be spoofed
Yes, if a bank logo appears

mod_02.text:
A message says:

"Your SIM expires tonight. Verify immediately."

Best action?
options: Contact your carrier using an official channel

mod_02.text:
Your friend's real Messenger account sends an unusual login link.

What may have happened?

Someone messages:

"Mom, new number. I lost my phone. Send ₱5,000."

Best verification?
options: Contact your mother through an existing trusted channel
Open the official app to review your transaction.
Reply with your OTP to cancel this transaction.
Visit a branch if you need assistance.

mod_02.text:
A QR code arrives by SMS for "account verification."

What should you do?
options: Scan it while using mobile data
Verify through the official service instead
Scan it but don't type anything

mod_02.text:
A message correctly identifies your name and recent online purchase.

Does that prove legitimacy?
options: Only if the amount is correct
Yes, because scammers do not know purchase information
No; personal information can be leaked or obtained elsewhere

mod_02.text:
A sender claims to be your bank and provides a link using HTTPS.

What does HTTPS prove?
options: The connection to that website is encrypted, not that the site is legitimate
The site has been approved by the bank
Your OTP is safe to enter
Opening your bank's official app independently
Calling the number contained in the message
Checking whether the sender knows your name

mod_02.text: What feature connects most smishing attacks?
options: They attempt to trigger an unsafe action through a message

mod_03.text:
A bank caller asks for your OTP.

What should you do?
Can caller ID alone prove who is calling?

A caller demands payment using gift cards to avoid arrest.

What is most likely?

A caller says:

"Do not hang up or your account will be permanently closed."

What tactic is being used?

Someone claiming to be IT support asks for remote access to your computer.

Safest response?

A caller knows your full name.

What does this prove?
options: Very little; names can be publicly available or leaked

mod_03.text:
A caller claiming to be your bank asks for your CVV.

Best response?
options: Provide it if they know your name
Refuse and contact the bank independently

mod_03.text:
You receive a suspicious call from a displayed bank number.

How should you verify it?
options: Call the official number from your card or bank app
Ask the caller to send an SMS

mod_03.text:
A caller creates panic and repeatedly prevents you from hanging up.

Why?
options: To keep your phone connected technically
To reduce the time you have to think and verify

mod_03.text:
Someone claiming to be the registrar asks for your portal password.

Best response?
options: Verify with the registrar through an official channel

mod_03.text:
A caller sounds exactly like a family member asking for emergency money.

What should you do?
options: Verify using another established contact method
Ask them to repeat your name

mod_03.text:
A caller knows your name, school and date of birth.

What is the correct conclusion?
options: Information knowledge alone does not prove identity
It is safe to provide an OTP

mod_03.text: Why is "stay on the line and don't tell anyone" especially suspicious?
options: Calls longer than five minutes are fraudulent

mod_03.text: What principle best protects against vishing?
options: Never rely solely on information provided by the caller to verify the caller
Only trust callers who know personal information
Creating a believable fake identity or story to obtain information/access

mod_04.text:
Someone wearing an IT uniform asks for your password.

What should you do?
options: Give it because of the uniform
Verify their identity and authorization independently
Ask another student to give theirs first

mod_04.text:
A stranger claims to be a student's parent and asks for private records.

Safest action?
options: Ask whether they know the student's birthday

mod_04.text: Why do attackers often impersonate authority figures?
options: Authority can make victims more likely to comply
Emails from managers cannot be blocked

mod_04.text:
Someone claims:

"I'm the Dean's assistant. Send the student list immediately."

What should you do?

A person knows your supervisor's name and office number.

Does this establish authorization?
options: Only if they know your name too

mod_04.text:
A delivery worker asks to enter a restricted room.

What matters most?
options: Whether they are authorized to enter

mod_04.text: What should you verify first when someone requests sensitive information?
options: Their authority and legitimate need for the information

mod_04.text:
A "researcher" asks for your account password to complete a survey.

Best response?
options: Give only the username and password hint

mod_04.text: Which is a common characteristic of pretexting?
options: A believable story explaining why information or access is needed

mod_04.text:
An employee says their badge stopped working and asks you to let them inside.

Best response?
options: Ask for their employee name only

mod_04.text:
An attacker has researched your organization and knows several real employee names.

Why does this strengthen pretexting?
options: It proves the attacker works there
Accurate details make a fabricated story more believable

mod_04.text:
A senior manager tells you to bypass normal security because the request is urgent.

What should you do?
options: Follow the request because they outrank you
Follow the required security process or seek formal authorization
Do it and report it later

mod_04.text: Which question is most important when evaluating a request?
options: "Is this person independently verified and authorized to request this?"

mod_04.text: What is the fundamental weakness exploited by pretexting?
options: People's willingness to trust believable identities and stories

mod_05.text: What makes baiting different from many other attacks?
options: It offers something attractive to encourage unsafe behavior

mod_05.text:
You find a USB labeled "Final Exam Answers."

Safest action?
options: Turn it in without connecting it

mod_05.text:
A site offers expensive software completely free from an unknown source.

What is the main risk?
options: Free software cannot run on Windows

mod_05.text:
A pop-up says:

"Congratulations! You won a new phone!"

What technique may be involved?
Why might an attacker label a USB "Salary Information"?

A file is named:

FreeMovie.mp4.exe

What is its actual executable extension?
Why can pirated software be dangerous?
options: Modified installers can hide malicious code
Pirated programs cannot connect to the internet

mod_05.text:
A QR code on a poster promises free Wi-Fi.

Safest response?
options: Verify the Wi-Fi details with an official source

mod_05.text:
A stranger gives students free USB drives.

What is the key security concern?
options: They may contain malicious files or programs
The USB may be too small

mod_05.text: Which is the best example of baiting?
options: "Give me your OTP or your account will close."
An attacker pretending to be IT
A USB labeled "Confidential Exams" deliberately left in a hallway

mod_05.text:
Someone sends you a "free premium game" installer.

Before running it, what is most important?
options: Whether it came from a trusted and authorized source
Whether your friend likes the game
Whether the file size is small

mod_05.text: What do malicious USBs, free downloads, prize links and enticing QR codes have in common?
options: They exploit curiosity or desire to trigger unsafe actions

mod_05.text:
A trusted friend gives you cracked software that works correctly on their computer.

What should you conclude?
options: It is safe if antivirus finds nothing
Your friend's computer proves its authenticity
Successful execution does not prove the software is free from malicious code

mod_05.text: Why is plugging a suspicious USB into an unused computer still unsafe?
options: Malicious code may still execute or spread
Unused computers cannot read USB devices

mod_05.text: Which best describes the defensive principle against baiting?
options: Do not let curiosity or rewards bypass normal trust and verification procedures
